summary: Defines the h323: URL scheme introduced in ITU-T H.323 version 4, which names an H.323 endpoint such as a person or service that can be called. The text reproduces the definition from H.323 so it is easy to find and so the scheme could be registered with IANA. It is an informational memo, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A web address tells your browser where a page lives. This memo describes a special kind of address for internet phone and video calls, so a link can say who to call. It writes the rules down in one easy place.

questions: how to call h323 from a web page
subtitle: A URL scheme for naming endpoints in H.323 video and audio calls.

tldr.problem: H.323 is a standard for audio and video calls over IP networks, but it had no standard way to encode an H.323 endpoint (a person, device, or service) as a URL that could be clicked or embedded in web pages.
tldr.mechanism: The h323: URL scheme encodes a user alias and optional host information, allowing an H.323 entity to be named in the same way as web pages are named with http: URLs.
tldr.outcome: The scheme was defined in ITU-T Recommendation H.323 version 4 and is published as this RFC for IANA registration and easy reference.

today: This RFC documents the h323: URL scheme for IANA registration. The scheme was defined in ITU-T Recommendation H.323 version 4 (November 2000) and remains part of the H.323 standard. It allows H.323 applications to be invoked from web pages and documents, and is used in H.323-aware web browsers and collaboration platforms.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
H.323 is the ITU-T standard for packet-based multimedia communications—audio and video calls over IP networks like the internet. Version 4 of the H.323 standard introduced a new URL scheme called h323: to identify H.323 endpoints that can be called or receive services.

This RFC reproduces the H323-URL definition from ITU-T Recommendation H.323 itself. It is published as an RFC for ease of access to the internet community and to register the h323: scheme with IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority), ensuring that the scheme name is not duplicated or claimed by another protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Video phone calls need addresses, just like phone calls have phone numbers. This memo writes down what an H.323 address looks like so everyone is talking about the same thing.

sections.title: URL Syntax and Encoding
sections.content:
The h323: URL has the form h323:address[parameters]. The address can be a user alias alone, a hostport alone, or a user alias followed by an at-sign (@) and a hostport (similar to an email address). The hostport is the domain name, IP address (IPv4 or IPv6), or port where the H.323 endpoint can be reached.

For example: h323:alice names an alias; h323:alice@gatekeeper.example.com names an alias at a specific gatekeeper; h323:192.0.2.1:1720 is a direct IP address with a port. The user field is a Unicode string encoded in UTF-8 and then percent-escaped as necessary. Characters below 0x80 in the user field are case-insensitive; characters 0x80 and above are case-sensitive. The host part is always case-insensitive.

Optional parameters can be appended to the URL using the semicolon notation (similar to HTTP query parameters). The specific parameter definitions are left for future work, but the syntax reserves space for them. For example: h323:alice@example.com;param=value.
sections.plainLanguage: The address has a name part (who you want to call), optionally followed by an @ and a location part (where they are). Some characters may be encoded as percent-signs with numbers.

sections.title: Addressing and Endpoint Resolution
sections.content:
The h323: URL is designed to help resolve the address of an H.323 endpoint, which may be a user, a device (such as an IP phone), or a service. The user portion is an alias for the entity without carrying location information. This is useful because an H.323 endpoint can move between networks or devices without changing its alias. The hostport specifies where to direct calls—the domain name, gatekeeper, border element, or other functional element responsible for the endpoint.

An h323: URL can represent a simple endpoint like h323:alice (just an alias, with no location specified), which would require external directory lookup to resolve. Or it can be explicit like h323:alice@gatekeeper.company.com, which specifies both the alias and the gatekeeper that knows about that alias. Different applications and directories may use these forms differently.
sections.plainLanguage: The h323: address can just be a name (like a nickname), or it can include where to find that person on the network.

sections.title: Applications and Deployment
sections.content:
The h323: URL is intended to help resolve the address of another H.323 entity, which may be a user, a device (like an IP phone), or a service. The user portion is an alias for the entity without carrying location information; the hostport is the domain name, gatekeeper, border element, or other functional element to which calls may be directed.

H.323 URLs can be carried by other protocols such as SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) or TRIP (Telephony Routing over IP). They can be embedded in web pages or XML data for H.323 applications to use when initiating calls or requesting services. When embedded in web pages, an h323: link acts like an http: link, allowing users to click to initiate a call to that endpoint.

Security for H.323 URLs transmitted within H.323 protocols is addressed by the H.235 security framework. When h323: URLs are carried in other protocols like SIP, the security mechanisms of those protocols apply. This document does not define new security requirements, as security is the responsibility of the calling context.
sections.plainLanguage: You can put an h323: address in a web page just like you put http: addresses, and someone can click it to call that person or service.
